Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The people responsible have faced no consequences
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Body Shame' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile for a civilian-in-war-zone trauma unless there is some indication of bodily violation, injury, or humiliation. The other selected items center on injustice, impunity, hypervigilance, dissociative/fragmented memory, and avoidance, but provide no supporting context for body-focused shame, making this item stand out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The Threat items emphasize pervasive current danger and hypervigilance (scanning exits, needing to stay alert at night), but the formulation specifically has Triggers → Threat inactive. In this profile, Triggers are concrete reminders such as car sounds and related media, yet the Threat items are generalized and not plausibly linked to those triggers; this makes the threat presentation feel disconnected from the trigger pattern.

vignette:
Kham was seventy-four, a wiry man whose hands had the permanent tremor of old burns and a life spent gripping a welding torch. He had been a civilian in a village in central Vietnam when the fighting came. His family fled toward the river as trucks rumbled down the dirt road, the sound of their engines mixing with shouting and artillery. He remembered the heat, the dust, the way his chest had seized as he tried to pull his youngest child into a ditch—breathless, legs frozen. He had let go. He had hidden. He did not know what happened to that child after the trucks passed, and the memory ended there, a jagged tear in the film of that day. What he recalled made no sense—it felt like a story someone else had told him, too extreme to be real, and when he tried to put the pieces together, the picture would not hold. He blamed himself for the way he had acted, certain that if he had stayed instead of hidden, the outcome would have been different. And he was consumed by the injustice of it all: nothing had been done, no one had been held accountable, and the war had simply ended without ever addressing what happened in his village.

In the decades since, Kham had built a life in the United States as a welder, married, raising children in a quiet American town. But the old sounds followed him. A car backfiring outside his workshop sent his heart into his throat and his mind straight back to that ditch. The feeling of breathlessness that sometimes came when he bent over a steel beam—from age, from welding fumes—would suddenly feel like the same panic, and he would have to step outside, gasping. He had stopped watching the news years ago, because any footage of conflict made the memory surge back, and it always felt unreal, as if it belonged to someone else. Once the memory had taken hold, even harmless sounds—a car door closing, a distant shout, the hum of a welding machine—became signals he could no longer trust, each one demanding an urgent response. When the memory broke through, it did not feel like the past; it felt like the threat had returned to the present, and he would find himself tensed, looking for cover, convinced that danger was still just around the corner. He told himself to think of something else when the images intruded, redirecting his thoughts to his work or his wife, but that required constant effort, and he was always tired.

The fatigue came partly from sleep. He had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert, listening for trucks that never came. During the day, he was hypervigilant in a way that his colleagues called “jumpy.” That constant vigilance meant that ordinary sounds—the clatter of a falling tool, the rumble of a delivery truck, the bang of a door—no longer felt neutral; each one demanded his full attention, as if it might be the first sign that danger had finally arrived. He found it hard to concentrate on his welding blueprints, because his attention kept scanning the parking lot for movement. The sound of a car pulling in, especially a heavy one, would make his hands pause. He had come to believe that the world was still dangerous, that the people who had done this had never been punished, and that he himself was partly responsible. Because he was certain the world was unsafe and that he bore some of the blame, he began to see threat in ordinary events—a stranger walking too slowly past his gate, the rumble of a far-off engine, even the clang of a dropped tool—each one feeling like a warning he could not afford to ignore. Those appraisals kept his guard up: if he stopped being watchful, something terrible would happen again.

Because the memory felt so partial and alien, he avoided talking about the war with anyone, even his wife. When she asked, he changed the subject or simply left the room. The more he redirected and refused to speak, the more the memory seemed to slip into a strange, dissociated place—more alien, less believable, yet more intrusive. The lack of a coherent story also fed his self-blame: if he could not fully remember what he did, then maybe he was guilty of something worse. And his avoidance of open spaces, born from the dash to the river, meant he stayed inside his small workshop or his home, rarely walking in the park or even his own backyard unless he had a clear line of sight to every door.

His wife had begun to worry. She noticed he flinched at car sounds during their drives, and that he seemed to be losing weight because he was too vigilant to eat. He knew his concentration was slipping, and he had nearly dropped a hot steel beam last month. That scared him. What finally brought him to the clinic was his daughter’s wedding next spring. He wanted to be there, but he was terrified of the open lawn, the possible cars, the speeches that might make him think of the past. He was afraid he would spiral into that incomplete, unreal memory in front of everyone. Most of all, he was afraid that nothing would ever change, that the injustice would never be acknowledged, and that he would carry this alone until the end. But he came anyway, hoping that maybe, for the first time, he could talk about that day without the story dissolving.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not explicitly state that negative appraisals (e.g., self-blame, world is dangerous) cause or influence the occurrence of triggers; it only shows triggers leading to appraisals.
No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory directly leads to a sense of threat; threat appears linked to appraisals rather than the memory itself.
There is no causal relationship where the memory itself produces or influences the experience of triggers; triggers are instead described as external stimuli that evoke the memory.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly state that negative appraisals (e.g., self-blame, world is dangerous) cause or influence the occurrence of triggers; it only shows triggers leading to appraisals.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Threat: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory directly leads to a sense of threat; threat appears linked to appraisals rather than the memory itself.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Triggers: There is no causal relationship where the memory itself produces or influences the experience of triggers; triggers are instead described as external stimuli that evoke the memory.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
